newsitem.title: USA: U.S. financial regulators seek Internet cures.
newsitem.headline: U.S. financial regulators seek Internet cures.

text.p: The U.S. financial industry and regulators are groping for cures for headaches created by the growing use of the Internet, industry executives said on Thursday.

"Just as the industry will have to be flexible to take advantage of those (opportunities), regulators are facing a critical challenge," Kristen Geyer, special counsel for market regulation at the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), said at a Futures Industry Association conference.

"The key to making sure our regulations take up all the development...is for the industry and regulators to work together to identify the issues early so that we can coordinate efforts to address them flexibly," she said.

More than 17 brokerages offer electronic trading to retail customers, with more than 800,000 on-line investors, Geyer said. Many more firms offer information on their Websites and the use of E-mail is expanding rapidly.
Besides committing fraud, firms could inadvertently violate regulations, perhaps somewhere abroad if not in their home countries, industry officials said.
"Once you advertise securities or services on Internet, the accessibility of the advertisement alone can trigger regulatory requirement in many jurisdictions," Geyer said.

Gary DeWaal, executive vice president of FIMAT Futures USA Inc, said that even if a firm had no Website, it could still be held liable if an associated broker overseas referred to it in sales material on the Net.
"It goes to show you that even if you're not on Internet...you have to be worried about it," he said.
The SEC's Geyer said so far there had been seven cases related to touting and potential fraud on the Internet, and the SEC had received constant enforcement tips or complaints.
Hoaxes and touting in so-called "chat rooms" were usually easy to track down, she said, adding that SEC could subpoena Internet service providers to identify culprits if need be.
Andrea Corcoran, director of Commodity Futures Trading Commission's (CFTC) trading and markets division, said the CFTC had "cybercops" surfing on the Net.
It even had pages with pictures and profiles of "wanted" persons, one of which was displayed as Corcoran spoke.
